introduction-the-push-and-pray-cycle.core: Slow CI breaks focus. Developers push, switch tasks and lose context, so fixes take longer and risky batching grows. Fast feedback is a safety feature, not a luxury.

first_principles.problem: A 40-minute pipeline means a typo costs an hour, so people batch changes and test less.
truths: Slow feedback encourages big, risky batches.
Feedback speed affects how often people test.

analogy.title: A surgeon waiting 15 minutes after each incision
analogy.story: Waiting to learn whether each cut was right would make surgery slower and more dangerous.
analogy.breaks: Speed shouldn't come from deleting meaningful tests.

example.title: The cost of a 40-minute pipeline

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: An hour lost to a 5-second mistake.

example.outcome: feedback speed is treated as core DevEx.

check.q: Why does slow CI make software less safe?
check.a: Developers batch more changes and test less often, increasing risk per change.

the-core-metric-time-to-feedback.core: Time to feedback is how long it takes to learn whether a change works. The inner loop (edit → run locally) should take seconds, and the outer loop (push → CI result) should take minutes. Optimise the outer loop by ordering fast checks first and parallelising.

first_principles.problem: Teams optimise total pipeline time but still make developers wait 20 minutes for a lint error.
truths: The first failure is the most useful signal.
derivation: **Fail fast**: lint, typecheck and unit tests first.

analogy.title: Airport security lines
analogy.story: Quick ID checks happen before slow bag scans, so problems surface early.
analogy.breaks: Parallelism costs money in runner minutes, so balance speed against cost.

example.title: Reordering a pipeline
flow: Before: build → e2e → lint (lint fails at 25 min)
After: lint ∥ unit (2 min) → build → e2e

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Most failures surface in under 3 minutes.

example.outcome: developers get answers while they still have context.

check.a: The local edit → build → test cycle on the developer's machine before pushing.

local-emulation-bringing-ci-to-the-lapto.core: When local and CI results disagree, developers waste push-and-wait cycles. Run the same containerised steps locally (act, Dagger, make targets, dev containers) so the inner loop predicts the outer one.

first_principles.problem: Tests pass locally but fail in CI because of different tool versions, env vars or OS, and you only find out after pushing.
truths: Containers can reproduce the CI environment.
The same entry points reduce drift.
derivation: Use the **same container images** locally and in CI.
Use **one entry point** (`make ci`, a Dagger function).
Use **act** to run GitHub workflows locally.
Keep **CI config thin** and the logic in scripts.

analogy.title: A flight simulator matching the real cockpit
analogy.story: Practice is only useful if the simulator behaves like the actual plane.
analogy.breaks: Some CI features (OIDC, hosted services) can't be fully emulated locally.

example.title: Thin CI YAML

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Local and CI produce identical results.

code.text:
jobs:
  ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: ghcr.io/acme/ci:2024.06
    steps: [ { uses: actions/checkout@v4 }, { run: make ci } ]
# locally: docker run --rm -v $PWD:/w -w /w ghcr.io/acme/ci:2024.06 make ci

example.outcome: the inner loop predicts CI outcomes.

check.a: So the real logic lives in scripts or make targets that can run identically on a laptop.

tool-spotlight-act-for-github-actions.core: `act` reads your .github/workflows files and runs jobs locally in Docker containers that mimic GitHub runners, so you can debug workflow logic without commit-push-wait loops.

first_principles.problem: Debugging a workflow YAML typo takes ten commits titled 'fix ci' and an hour of waiting.
truths: Workflow logic can be executed by any compatible runner.

analogy.title: A dress rehearsal at home
analogy.story: Run through the whole show in your living room before going to the real theatre.
analogy.breaks: act isn't a perfect replica: some actions, services and OIDC behave differently.

example.title: Debugging a matrix job locally

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Ten failed pushes become ten 30-second local runs.

code.text:
act -l                          # list jobs
act pull_request -j test --matrix python:3.12
act -s GITHUB_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)"

example.outcome: workflow changes are debugged in seconds.

check.q: What does `act` use to emulate GitHub runners?
